THE TRADITION OF RESPONSE - PART 2

WHAT THIS CHAPTER COVERS
- Evidence of the sense of the sacred in contemporary (today's) culture.
- Evidence of spirituality in contemporary culture.
- Non-religious responses to the questions of life: secular humanism, atheism, agnosticism, reductionism (Higher Level).
- Three key people in the humanist tradition: Erasmus, Karl Marx, Albert Camus - one key idea each.
- Two cosmologies of modern science: the Big Bang theory and the Expanding Universe theory (Higher Level), and how they might affect the search for meaning.

KEY TERMS
- Sacred: set apart as holy and connected with God.
- Sacred place: a place set apart where people celebrate religious beliefs and practices.
- Sacred time: a special time when members of religions gather to celebrate meaningful beliefs and practices.
- Sacred ceremonies: formal religious occasions celebrating part of a religious tradition.
- Sacred things: objects set apart for use in sacred ceremonies and rituals.
- Spiritual: relating to the human spirit rather than material or physical things; often linked with religious belief.
- Humanism: a rational outlook giving prime importance to human rather than divine or supernatural matters.
- Rational being: a being able to think sensibly or rationally.
- Reason: the power of the mind to think, understand and form judgements logically.
- Scepticism: a philosophy that denies the possibility of knowledge.
- Atheism: the denial of the existence of God.
- Agnosticism: the belief that we can only know what can be seen and understood using reason and science.
- Reductionism: reducing something down to its smallest parts.
- Renaissance: a period of cultural, artistic, political and economic change after the Middle Ages, in Europe from the fourteenth to the seventeenth century.
- Reformation: a sixteenth-century movement within Western Christianity that challenged the Catholic Church and especially papal authority.
- Second law of thermodynamics: a physical law that says every day the universe becomes more and more disordered.
- Entropy: a way of measuring disorder in a system (e.g. the universe).
- Thermodynamic equilibrium: a level of disorder that can go no further.
- Centrifugal effect: the apparent outward force felt by an object moving in a curved path, acting away from the centre of rotation.
- Astronomy: the study of everything in the universe beyond Earth's atmosphere.
- Cosmology: a branch of astronomy dealing with the origin and evolution of the universe.
- Political theorist: someone who builds or evaluates political theory, including political philosophy.

THE SENSE OF THE SACRED TODAY
- Sacred = that which is set aside for religious use. It takes many forms:
- Sacred places: River Ganges, Mecca, Bethlehem, churches, mosques, synagogues, temples.
- Sacred things: crucifix, prayer beads, the Bible, the Qur'an, blessed oils.
- Sacred ceremonies: the Sacraments, group prayer, weddings, funerals.
- Sacred times: Lent, Passover, Eid, Easter, Diwali.
- Chapter 4 showed our ancestors had a keen sense of the sacred. Question: will future generations think the twenty-first century was religious or secular?

STATISTICS - EUROPEAN VALUES STUDY (1981-2017)
- Tracks changing belief, practice and values in the Western world; five surveys measuring adults' sense of the sacred.
- Values are hard to measure, but the surveys are a rich source on how far a theistic (religious) way of life is accepted.
- Belief in God in 27 European countries (2008): in 17 of the 27, over 70% of adults believe in God - solid evidence of a sense of the sacred.
- Ireland, core Christian beliefs 1981-2008 (2008 was Ireland's last time in the survey): over 90% believe in God; over 70% in life after death; over 70% in heaven; just over 50% in hell; over 80% in sin. These figures stayed fairly constant over the years.
- Weekly attendance at religious services across 27 countries is quite low in many; highest in Poland, Ireland and Northern Ireland.
- Weekly attendance is often used to measure belief, but belief in God, heaven, hell and the afterlife may be a better measure of religious sensibility because it shows how far the spiritual dimension is appreciated.

CENSUS 2016 (IRELAND, CENTRAL STATISTICS OFFICE)
- Almost four million people identify with a religious tradition.
- Roman Catholics 3,729,115 (down 3.4%, average age 38.2).
- No religion 468,421 (up 73.6%, average age 34).
- Church of Ireland 126,414 (down 2.0%, average age 40.3).
- Muslim 63,443 (up 28.9%, average age 26).
- Orthodox 62,187 (up 37.5%, average age 30.2); Romanians are the largest group among Orthodox Christians (33.5%).
- Offaly has the highest % of Catholics (88.6%); Dun Laoghaire-Rathdown the lowest (69.9%).
- Dublin has 41.5% of all people with no religion; students had the largest 'no religion' response at 15.3% (up from 9.4% in 2011).
- Conclusion: religion and a sense of the sacred are still very relevant; the sense of the sacred crosses cultural and generational boundaries.

PILGRIMAGES TODAY
- Irish Times article by Patsy McGarry (7 June 2016): 'Popularity of pilgrimages endure despite drop in Mass attendance'.
- Weekly Mass attendance is dropping, but pilgrimages to Knock, Lough Derg and Croagh Patrick are as popular as ever; also local summer 'patterns' for patron saints.
- Knock: upwards of a million pilgrims a year.
- Croagh Patrick: 25,000-30,000 climb on the last Sunday of July each year.
- Lough Derg, Donegal: more arduous retreat; 18,000-20,000 pilgrims a year.
- Redemptorist novenas (nine days): up to 300,000 people at four June novenas - Mount St Alphonsus (Limerick), Esker Monastery (Athenry, Galway), St Michael's Church (Ballinasloe), Clonard Monastery (Belfast). Each has the icon of Our Lady of Perpetual Help (150th anniversary of its veneration). Fr Seamus Enright said the novenas 'have become a major religious event in themselves'.
- The Hajj: all Muslims who are physically and financially able must make the pilgrimage to Mecca, Saudi Arabia, at least once in their lifetime. 1997: 1.94 million; 2012: 3.16 million; 2018 estimated 2.28 million.

SPIRITUALITY TODAY
- Sacred assumes belief in God or gods. Spirituality acknowledges the 'otherness' or mysterious side of life and can include religious AND non-religious aspects. Everyone has a spirituality.
- You can be spiritual without being religious, but you cannot be religious without being spiritual.
- Being religious usually means belonging to an organised religion (e.g. Catholic, Hindu, Jewish): a community that worships a named God or gods, shares practices and rituals, accepts norms of behaviour, has recognised leaders and a sacred text (e.g. Bible, Torah).
- Some people now say they are spiritual but not religious - meaning a spiritual dimension in human life and nature beyond what we can see, feel or hear.
- Spirituality is about a person's inner being and the force at the centre of creation. People connect through mindfulness, music, poetry and the wonders of nature.
SPIRITUALITY IN PRACTICE
- Books on prayer and meditation in the Spirituality/Alternative section of bookshops.
- Openness to Eastern practices: meditation, yoga, mindfulness. In a noisy world, people need silence and stillness.
- Pope Francis: 'We all need to meditate, to reflect, to find ourselves.'
- Personal pilgrimages, e.g. to a loved one's grave or a special place of beauty.
- Nature as spiritual nourishment - wonder and awe; 'getting away from it all' is a modern-day retreat to nature.
- Acts of kindness and charity, e.g. checking on an elderly neighbour, volunteer organisations - many do this because it gives meaning to their lives.
- Paolo Coelho: 'It is the road that teaches us the best way to get there, and the road enriches us as we walk its length.'
THE CAMINO DE SANTIAGO
- Known in English as the Way of St James: a network of pilgrim routes to the shrine of the apostle St James the Great in the cathedral of Santiago de Compostela, Galicia, north-western Spain, where his remains are buried.
- Hundreds of thousands each year, Christians and non-Christians; mostly on foot, some by bicycle, horse or donkey; some walk for travel or sport; many see it as a spiritual retreat from modern life.
- Pilgrims completing it: 2010: 272,412; 2019: 347,578 (highest); 2020 (Covid-19): 54,155; 2021: 178,912.
- Fergal O'Keeffe, Tipperary Live (9 December 2021): the word he kept hearing was 'magical'.
- Guide Francisco Contreras: 'The Camino is not a transmission of faith but an exchange of ideas and a sharing of knowledge. The language of the Camino is love.'
- Guide Helder Cerejo: people do it for history, sport, a midlife crisis, religious pilgrimage, or to see the country - 'You can be yourself.'
- Journalist Catherine Murphy: complete freedom from normal life; phone off; it can be religious, healing and transformative, or about history.
- Teacher Jarlath O'Madain: strong bonds with strangers; 'you empty your heart to them'; 'the best thing I have ever done'.
- Author John Connell: 'you bring the question, and you bring the answer with you. The road allows you the time to think about the question, but the answer is inside yourself.' It is an internal journey; the real magic is the people you meet.
- Exam quote: John O'Donoghue, Anam Cara: 'There is an unprecedented spiritual hunger in our times.'

NON-RELIGIOUS RESPONSES TO THE QUESTIONS OF LIFE (HIGHER LEVEL)
- Religious people believe there is a sacred or 'other' dimension, mystery around human existence, and that humans are created and connected to their creator. This affects how they judge right and wrong and treat others and the earth.
- Other worldviews also seek meaning; they sometimes conflict with religion and sometimes speak to it.

HUMANISM
- There is nothing higher than or 'other' than human existence; everything needed for a good and dignified life is within the human person.
- This life is all we have; no life after death - so work at being happy and fulfilled now, and care about others' happiness.
- People are rational beings. Humanism does not speculate about a creator; it looks at life's questions through reason and science, with no reference to a higher power. Linked with 'free thinking'.
- Traced back to pre-Christian times (ancient Greece, Rome, medieval Europe). It flourished in the Renaissance (fourteenth to sixteenth centuries) - a time of rebirth in learning and new confidence in the person's ability to decide right and wrong.
- Early influential humanists were often people of deep faith; over time belief in God declined in humanism. (Image: Vitruvian Man by Leonardo da Vinci.)

SECULAR HUMANISM (SECULARISM)
- Origins in the Renaissance; took definite shape in the Enlightenment (seventeenth and eighteenth centuries).
- Purpose of life: to create a society that honours the dignity of all, achieved through reason alone. No goal of a blissful afterlife - fulfilment in this life.
- Great confidence in human reason to understand and order the world.
- Scepticism is an important element: questioning, withholding judgement, looking at all sides. A sceptic believes it is not possible to know the truth. Socrates is a great example - he claimed he knew nothing and used questioning and dialogue (Chapter 2).
- Science and reason are the ultimate source of knowledge and meaning; it does not believe in anything science cannot explain; no spiritual dimension.
- Human progress is measured by freedom from religious belief; religion is seen as superstition.
- Noted for its vision of an open, tolerant society and compassion for humanity.
- G. K. Chesterton: 'Reason is itself a matter of faith. It is an act of faith to assert that our thoughts have any relation to reality at all.'

ATHEISM
- The denial of the existence of God - by deliberate choice or by being unable to believe religious teachings.
- Theoretical atheism: denial based on incompatible ideas/theories, e.g. science and religion seen as incompatible, or the problem of evil and suffering makes belief in a loving God impossible.
- Practical atheism: the question of God is irrelevant to the person; also called religious indifference.
- Militant atheism: denial based on the idea that religious belief is harmful and restricts human potential.

AGNOSTICISM
- We can only know what can be seen and understood by reason and science - the position of 'not knowing' when something cannot be explained that way.
- Term first used by biologist Thomas Henry Huxley (1825-1895) in 1876. He was a contemporary and supporter of Charles Darwin, whose theory of evolution challenged Christian beliefs about creation. Huxley believed the question of a higher power is unsolved and insoluble.
- Today: people who believe evidence for or against God is inconclusive.
- Strict agnosticism: we can never know. Empirical agnosticism: we do not yet know.
- Agnosticism is a form of scepticism, which questions whether humans can know the truth, or whether there is such a thing as 'the truth'.

REDUCTIONISM
- Reducing something to its smallest parts. Began as a scientific method: e.g. from earth, air, fire and water to subatomic theory; astronomy moved from Earth at the centre to an ever-expanding universe of billions of galaxies.
- As a worldview: humans are part of the physical, natural world and no more. If something cannot be studied scientifically, it cannot be known. It rules out speculation, opinion, feeling, superstition and belief.
- Example: a sentence is just letters, spaces and punctuation; a novel just letters - but a novel explores great themes. A human is more than atoms and DNA. Reductionism denies we are more than the sum of our parts; higher meaning is lost.
- Consequences: demand for short, simple 'sound bite' news, a culture of convenience - risk of losing touch with complex realities like what it means to be human, justice and happiness.

KEY PERSON 1: DESIDERIUS ERASMUS (1466-1536)
- A great Renaissance humanist - ironically a cleric. A devout Christian but critical of the Church.
- Born in Rotterdam, Holland, 1466; orphaned young; joined an Augustinian monastery; ordained priest 1492; scholar who travelled widely in Europe.
- 1503-1511: published documents calling for spiritual renewal in the Church and society.
- Key idea: the power of education. He believed in the dignity of the human person; education is how humans improve and excel. 'People are not born, but formed.'
- Education trains the mind, aids moral and spiritual development and promotes civic virtues. Importance of the teacher, teaching method and the innate capacity to reach perfection. Parents and teachers have a duty to help children fulfil their potential.
- Without education humans have no humanity; education raises us above beasts. 'Man, unless he has experienced the influence of learning and philosophy, is at the mercy of impulses that are worse than those of a wild beast.'
- A well-educated child grows into 'a faithful protector of his family, a good husband to his wife, and a solid and useful citizen of his country'.
- Advocated scepticism about issues of the day, but did not question scripture as divinely inspired. Promoted Jesus Christ as the model of the human person. Criticised for humanist views but did not challenge the Church directly - a Christian humanist.
- Context: Martin Luther was questioning Church teaching, leading to the Reformation.

KEY PERSON 2: KARL MARX (1818-1883)
- Born in Treves (Trier), Germany, 1818. Journalist across Europe; took part in the French Revolution of 1848. More a political theorist than a philosopher.
- In London met Friedrich Engels, a factory manager who showed him the conditions of English workers. Wrote his most famous work, Das Kapital, in London.
- Key idea: meaning is found through work. The world is created by human work; human labour creates history. The only unchanging part of human nature is the inclination to work and produce.
- Historical materialism: a person's position in work and production decides their quality of life; humanity can be understood entirely through economics.
- Alienation: having no ownership or equal share in work, causing feelings of not belonging and powerlessness - when masses work for little or no wage and a few control production and take most of the profit. This is the main source of inequality and suffering.
- Vision: a fair society according to people's abilities and needs; collective ownership and shared responsibility; respect for human dignity; an egalitarian, peaceful society.
- Rejected religion; human reason and consciousness are most important; the struggle for freedom makes us human; no one should be a slave to any system - work or religion.
- Drawbacks of Marxism: discredits religion (may limit freedom to worship); state controls everything including education (limited education, no academic freedom for teachers); limits private property (may affect where you live and privacy); discourages entrepreneurship - no individual incentive, could lead to a stagnant society. Shared ownership arguably costs personal freedom.

KEY PERSON 3: ALBERT CAMUS (1913-1960)
- French Algerian, born into a poor working-class family; lived on the margins, so sensitive to discrimination by class and religion.
- Born as World War I began; died not long after World War II. Developed a philosophy committed to transforming daily life from the absurd to the meaningful.
- Key idea: the absurdity of life - the feeling that life has no meaning. This is called existential humanism.
- Life can feel absurd because of deadening routine, awareness that death is inevitable, questioning life's purpose, or isolation from others. Question: how can one live authentically in a world without meaning?
- Explored through three novels:
- The Outsider (The Stranger): Meursault, an Algerian man, indifferent to everything - does not cry at his mother's funeral, barely reacts to being convicted. Facing execution: 'Nothing, nothing had the least importance ... all alike would be condemned to die one day'. Death reveals life's absurdity. Awareness of absurdity frees him from pretence: 'I laid my heart open to the benign indifference of the universe ... made me realise that I'd been happy, and that I was happy still.' Camus refuses to accept that one cannot be happy.
- The Plague: a plague hits a city in Algiers; authorities fail, so citizens join together to fight it. Man is a healer with a role. Narrator Rieux: 'there are more things to admire in man than to despise'. Theme: human solidarity - a bond uniting all humans against evil and suffering.
- The Fall (1956): lawyer Jean Baptiste Clemence sees a woman jump off a bridge (Pont Royal, Paris) and does nothing; he then sees all his past good deeds as a sham done for praise. Explores forgiveness in an absurd world; Camus concludes repentance is in vain because there is no forgiveness. 'God is not needed to create guilt or to punish. Our fellow men suffice, aided by ourselves ... I have known what is worse, the judgement of men.' Deeply pessimistic about the inhumanity in every person.
- Camus believed a meaningful society comes when each person's dignity and human intelligence are respected. He linked 'despair' with the decline of traditional religion, and believed there is an inbuilt desire to fight despair and bring transformation. Rebellion against oppression shows the human desire for dignity.
- Awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature three years before his sudden death at forty-six.

SCIENCE AND RELIGION (HIGHER LEVEL)
- Late twentieth-century discoveries changed theories about space, time and matter.
- Historically religion and science had a strained relationship. Religion answered: how was the universe created? How will it end? How was life created? Does it have a purpose?
- Nicolaus Copernicus (1473-1543), mathematician, laid foundations for modern physics and astronomy: the earth revolves around the sun and rotates on its axis. This conflicted with the religious view that humans and the earth were the centre of God's creation; his supporters suffered before it was accepted.
- Science seeks a rational explanation for everything; religion accepts there isn't always one and is open to mystery. They start from different points but can work together.
- George V. Coyne SJ, Jesuit priest and astronomer ('Quantum Cosmology and Creation'): conflicts are 'temporary and apparent' and can spur a 'richer unified understanding'. In Modern Cosmology and Life's Meaning he says the best cosmology does not claim to have the ultimate answers; 'certainties lie always in the future'.
- Psalm 19:1: 'The heavens are telling the glory of God; and the firmament proclaims his handiwork.'
- Brian Cox (physicist): we are 'atoms contemplating atoms'; 'We are the cosmos made conscious and life is the means by which the universe understands itself.'
- Cosmology is about all space and all time - everything that was, is, or will be.
- Science's first question: was there a creation event or has the universe always existed? If it always existed, it is ageless; if it began, there was once nothing then something - so what caused it?

COSMOLOGY 1: THE BIG BANG THEORY
- Creation event about 13.8 billion years ago, when the universe exploded into existence. Developed by George Lemaitre, a Catholic priest.
- Based on the second law of thermodynamics: every day the universe becomes more disordered. The most important law for understanding the universe's evolution and the passage of time.
- 1850: physicist Rudolf Clausius devised entropy - a measure of disorder.
- Brian Cox (BBC, Wonders of the Universe): mortar crumbles, glass shatters, buildings collapse. Sandcastle example: a pile of sand can be rearranged trillions of ways; a sandcastle has the same grains but order; almost anything (wind, someone knocking it) will make it disordered. So entropy always increases because it is overwhelmingly more likely.
- This explains why time runs one way - the Arrow of Time. Events never go backwards; changes can never be undone. Cox: in the universe, as in our lives, 'everything is irreversibly changing'.
- Babies born and new buildings seem to restore order, but the law applies to the system as a whole: order in one place creates disorder elsewhere; some energy is lost forever.
- A system reaches thermodynamic equilibrium (disorder can go no further). So: (1) the universe will die; (2) it cannot have existed forever, or it would already have reached its end. Therefore there was a creation event.
- The earth's core temperature shows the earth is about four and a half billion years old; the sun is a little older and is using up its fuel.
- Gravity: Isaac Newton showed gravity is a universal force. Planets and stars don't crash because they revolve and the galaxy rotates - the centrifugal effect, like balls in a turning roulette wheel. Something must have set the motion going - again pointing to a creation event.

COSMOLOGY 2: THE EXPANDING UNIVERSE THEORY
- In the 1920s American astronomer Edwin Hubble found the galaxies are moving apart, not falling together.
- If the universe is expanding, it must once have been smaller. The expansion rate is decelerating (slowing), supporting an initial explosion.
- Space was created in the Big Bang, and because space and time are linked, time began then too - space and time exploded out of nothing.
- Heat radiating from space is the leftover heat of the Big Bang.
- The Big Bang is widely accepted by scientists and welcomed by most religious thinkers. No agreement on how the universe will end; science has not yet found the cause of creation.

THE FATE OF THE UNIVERSE AND MEANING
- Big Chill: galaxies thin out, the universe cools, energy dissipates (entropy), stars go out, temperature reaches absolute zero - a long cosmic night. Over 150 billion years left.
- Big Crunch: expansion stops; gravity drags everything back; the universe heats up and collapses into a tiny, infinitely dense, hot pellet - perhaps ready for another Big Bang. As little as 10-20 billion years left.
- Two facts: the universe had a beginning and it will die. Challenge: how can it be meaningful if it will explode or implode?
- Fine tuning / anthropic principle: the universe is meant to contain intelligent life able to understand it; everything is adjusted within such a narrow range that it seems the result of care, not chance (e.g. gravity, star energy, speed of expansion - slightly different and no life). Trent Horn: the odds are like finding a randomly marked atom in the universe.
- Effect on meaning: may challenge belief in God as creator, or lead people to see God as first cause - St Thomas Aquinas's 'uncreated creator'.
- Wonder: Nellie McLaughlin, Out of Wonder - all creation sings 'the song that is the universe'; we are cosmic beings.
- Pope Francis, Laudato si': 'Each being is unique in the magnificent web of life ... everything is, as it were, a caress of God' (LS 84); the world is 'a joyful mystery to be contemplated with gladness and praise' (LS 12), not a problem to be solved.
- This wonder could inspire care for the earth and action on the climate crisis - to be true stewards.
- Richard Feynman: American theoretical physicist, Nobel Prize for Physics 1965; Bill Gates called him 'the best teacher I never had'. In summer 1955 he wrote a poem: earth was once a dead planet; molecules formed complex patterns; DNA and protein; finally 'atoms with consciousness; matter with curiosity ... wonders at wondering: I a universe of atoms an atom in the Universe.'

rows.prompt: Which of these is an example of a sacred time?
rows.explanation: Lent, Passover, Eid, Easter and Diwali are given as examples of sacred times.

rows.prompt: In how many of the 27 European countries did over 70% of adults believe in God (2008)?
rows.explanation: The European Values Study found over 70% belief in God in seventeen of the twenty-seven countries.

rows.prompt: According to the European Values Study, what percentage of Irish adults believe in God?
rows.explanation: Over 90% of Irish adults believe in God; belief in hell is just over 50%.

rows.prompt: Why might belief in God, heaven and the afterlife be a better measure of religious sensibility than Mass attendance?
options: It is easier to count in a census
It shows how far the spiritual dimension is valued
It is not affected by religion
rows.explanation: Belief in these things gives evidence of how much the spiritual dimension of life is appreciated.

rows.prompt: About how many pilgrims visit Knock each year?
rows.explanation: Knock attracts upwards of a million pilgrims a year.

rows.prompt: Where does the Camino de Santiago end?
options: The cathedral of Santiago de Compostela
rows.explanation: The Way of St James leads to the shrine of St James the Great in Santiago de Compostela, Spain.

rows.prompt: Which statement about religion and spirituality does the chapter make?
options: You can be religious without being spiritual
Spirituality always needs a sacred text
You can be spiritual without being religious
Only religious people have a spirituality
rows.explanation: You can be spiritual without being religious, but you can't be religious without being spiritual.

rows.prompt: Which author said 'you bring the question, and you bring the answer with you' about the Camino?
rows.explanation: John Connell said the road gives time to think but the answer is inside yourself.

rows.prompt: What is the basic position of humanism?
options: Nothing is higher than human existence
rows.explanation: Humanism holds that there is nothing higher than or 'other' than human existence.

rows.prompt: In which period did humanism flourish?
rows.explanation: Humanism flourished between the fourteenth and sixteenth centuries, the Renaissance.

rows.prompt: How does secularism view religious belief?
rows.explanation: Secularism sees religious belief as superstition that science and reason make unnecessary.

rows.prompt: Which type of atheism is also called religious indifference?
rows.explanation: Practical atheism denies God because the question is of no relevance to the person.

rows.prompt: A person rejects God because they think religion is harmful and limits human potential. Which type of atheism is this?
rows.explanation: Militant atheism denies God on the basis that religious belief is harmful and restricts human potential.

rows.prompt: Who first used the term 'agnostic' in 1876?
rows.explanation: Biologist Thomas Henry Huxley, a supporter of Darwin, first used the term in 1876.

rows.prompt: What is the difference between strict and empirical agnosticism?
options: God exists versus God does not exist
Science is true versus religion is true
We can never know versus we do not yet know
We know God versus we feel God
rows.explanation: Strict agnostics say we can never know; empirical agnostics say we do not yet know.

rows.prompt: According to reductionism, what is a novel?
options: A collection of letters and no more
A symbol of the human spirit
rows.explanation: Reductionism reduces everything to its parts, so a novel is just a collection of letters - and higher meaning is lost.

rows.prompt: What was the key idea of Desiderius Erasmus?
rows.explanation: Erasmus believed education was the means through which humans could improve and excel.

rows.prompt: Which quote belongs to Erasmus?
options: There are more things to admire in man than to despise
Reason is itself a matter of faith
People are not born, but formed
rows.explanation: Erasmus believed 'People are not born, but formed' - through education.

rows.prompt: Who introduced Karl Marx to the conditions of English workers?
rows.explanation: In London Marx met Friedrich Engels, a factory manager.

rows.prompt: What did Marx call the theory that a person's place in work decides their quality of life?
rows.explanation: Historical materialism holds that humanity can be understood entirely through economics and work.

rows.prompt: What did Marx mean by alienation?
options: Having no ownership or equal share in work
Living as an outsider in a foreign land
rows.explanation: Alienation is having no sense of ownership or equal participation in work, leading to powerlessness.

rows.prompt: What name is given to Camus' philosophy that life can seem absurd?
rows.explanation: Camus' sense of the absurd - the feeling that life has no meaning - is called existential humanism.

rows.prompt: In which Camus novel do citizens unite because the authorities fail them?
rows.explanation: In The Plague citizens come together to fight the plague, showing human solidarity.

rows.prompt: In The Fall, why does Jean Baptiste Clemence feel morally bankrupt?
options: He did not cry at his mother's funeral
He did nothing as a woman jumped off a bridge
He was convicted of a serious crime
He failed to stop a plague
rows.explanation: After failing to help the woman, he saw all his good deeds as a sham done for praise.

rows.prompt: Who developed the Big Bang theory?
rows.explanation: The Big Bang theory was developed by George Lemaitre, a Catholic priest.

rows.prompt: What is entropy?
options: The force that holds planets together
The speed at which galaxies move apart
The heat left over from the Big Bang
A way of measuring disorder in a system
rows.explanation: Entropy, devised by Rudolf Clausius in 1850, measures disorder within a system.

rows.prompt: Why does thermodynamic equilibrium suggest the universe has not existed forever?
options: Its galaxies would have stopped moving
It would already have reached its end stage
The sun would be younger than the earth
rows.explanation: If the universe had always existed it would have reached thermodynamic equilibrium long ago.

rows.prompt: What does the roulette wheel example explain?
options: The centrifugal effect keeping planets apart
Why time runs in one direction
rows.explanation: Like balls in a turning wheel, planets stay in place because of rotation; something must have started it.

rows.prompt: What did Edwin Hubble discover in the 1920s?
options: The earth goes around the sun
rows.explanation: Hubble found galaxies were not falling together but moving apart - the Expanding Universe theory.

rows.prompt: What is the 'Big Crunch'?
options: The universe cooling to absolute zero
The universe collapsing back into a tiny hot pellet
rows.explanation: In the Big Crunch expansion stops and gravity drags everything back together.

rows.prompt: What does the anthropic principle claim?
options: Humans are just atoms and DNA
The universe is fine-tuned for intelligent life
rows.explanation: It says the universe is adjusted so precisely that it seems the result of care, not chance.

rows.prompt: Give two pieces of evidence that there is still a sense of the sacred in Ireland today.
rows.model_answer: The European Values Study found that over 90% of Irish adults believe in God and over 70% believe in life after death and heaven. Census 2016 showed almost four million people identify with a religious tradition. Pilgrimages are as popular as ever, with upwards of a million visiting Knock each year and 25,000-30,000 climbing Croagh Patrick.

rows.prompt: Explain the difference between being religious and being spiritual.
rows.model_answer: Being religious usually means belonging to an organised religion with a named God, shared rituals, norms, leaders and a sacred text. Being spiritual means recognising the 'otherness' or mysterious side of life and connecting with one's inner being, which can be religious or non-religious. You can be spiritual without being religious, but not religious without being spiritual.

rows.prompt: Name two ways people express spirituality in today's world.
rows.model_answer: People practise Eastern practices like meditation, yoga and mindfulness to find silence and stillness in a noisy world. Others find spiritual nourishment in nature, or express spirituality through acts of kindness and charity, such as checking on an elderly neighbour or volunteering. Pilgrimages like the Camino de Santiago are another example.

rows.prompt: Explain what secular humanism believes about the purpose of life.
rows.model_answer: Secular humanism, which took shape in the Enlightenment, believes the purpose of life is to create a society that honours the dignity of all, using reason alone. It does not believe in an afterlife, so it focuses on fulfilment in this life. It trusts science and reason as the source of knowledge and sees religion as superstition.

rows.prompt: Name and explain the three types of atheism.
rows.model_answer: Theoretical atheism denies God because of incompatible ideas, such as believing science and religion clash or that evil and suffering rule out a loving God. Practical atheism, or religious indifference, sees the question of God as irrelevant. Militant atheism denies God because it sees religious belief as harmful and restricting human potential.

rows.prompt: Explain why reductionism can cause problems when applied to the meaning of life.
rows.model_answer: Reductionism says humans are only part of the physical world and that what cannot be studied scientifically cannot be known. By reducing everything to its parts, higher meaning is lost - a human becomes just atoms and DNA, a novel just letters. It denies we are more than the sum of our parts, so complex realities like justice, happiness and what it means to be human can be lost.

rows.prompt: Outline Karl Marx's key idea about work.
rows.model_answer: Marx believed meaning is found through work and that human labour creates history; the one unchanging part of human nature is the urge to work and produce. His theory of historical materialism says your position in work decides your quality of life. He saw alienation in work, where many earn little while a few control production and profits, as the main source of inequality and suffering.

rows.prompt: Explain how Camus' thinking developed from The Outsider to The Plague.
rows.model_answer: In The Outsider, Meursault is indifferent to everything and death shows life is absurd, but awareness of this frees him from pretence and he finds he is happy. In The Plague, Camus still sees the world as absurd but shows how to live in it: citizens unite to fight the plague, and the narrator Rieux says there are more things to admire in man than to despise. This shows a move to the humanist ideal of human solidarity.

rows.prompt: Explain how the second law of thermodynamics points to a creation event.
rows.model_answer: The law says the universe becomes more disordered every day, and entropy measures this disorder. A system eventually reaches thermodynamic equilibrium, where disorder can go no further. So the universe will die, and it cannot have existed forever, because it would already have reached that end stage. Therefore there must have been a beginning, a creation event.

rows.prompt: 'There is an unprecedented spiritual hunger in our times.' (John O'Donoghue, Anam Cara). Outline how a search for the spiritual is evident in society today.
rows.model_answer:
Spirituality acknowledges the 'otherness' or mysterious side of life and can be religious or non-religious. Even though weekly Mass attendance is falling, there is clear evidence of a spiritual hunger today.

First, pilgrimage remains hugely popular. Knock attracts upwards of a million pilgrims a year, 25,000-30,000 climb Croagh Patrick on the last Sunday of July, and up to 300,000 attend the Redemptorist June novenas. The Camino de Santiago, the Way of St James to Santiago de Compostela in Spain, had 347,578 pilgrims in 2019. Many walkers are not Christian but see it as a spiritual retreat from modern life. John Connell said the road gives you time to think about the question, 'but the answer is inside yourself'.

Second, there is an openness to Eastern practices like meditation, yoga and mindfulness. In a crowded, noisy world people seek silence and stillness; Pope Francis says 'We all need to meditate, to reflect, to find ourselves.' Bookshops have whole sections on prayer and meditation.

Third, people find spiritual nourishment in nature, retreating to places of beauty that fill them with wonder and awe, and they express spirituality through acts of kindness and charity, such as volunteering, because it gives meaning to their lives.

rows.prompt: Compare the approach that would be taken by agnosticism and reductionism when answering a question about the meaning of life.
rows.model_answer:
Agnosticism is the belief that we can only know what can be seen and understood through reason and science. The term was first used by Thomas Henry Huxley in 1876, a supporter of Darwin, who believed the question of a higher power was unsolved and insoluble. Asked about the meaning of life, an agnostic would say that the evidence for or against God is inconclusive. A strict agnostic would say we can never know whether there is a God-given purpose; an empirical agnostic would say we do not yet know. Agnosticism is a form of scepticism.

Reductionism reduces everything to its smallest parts. As a worldview it holds that humans are part of the physical world and no more, and that if something cannot be studied scientifically it cannot be known. A reductionist would answer the question of meaning only in physical terms: a human is a collection of atoms and DNA, just as a novel is a collection of letters.

Similarity: both rely on reason and science as the only way to know. Difference: the agnostic stays open, leaving the question of God and ultimate meaning unanswered, while the reductionist closes it, denying that there is any 'more' beyond our physical parts, so any higher meaning is lost.

rows.prompt: Outline the approach taken by two key people in the humanist tradition with regard to the human search for the meaning of life.
rows.model_answer:
Desiderius Erasmus (1466-1536) was a Renaissance humanist and an Augustinian priest. His key idea was the power of education. He believed in the dignity of the human person and that education is the way humans improve and excel: 'People are not born, but formed.' Without education, he said, humans are at the mercy of impulses worse than a wild beast. Education trains the mind, supports moral and spiritual growth and makes good citizens, and parents and teachers have a duty to help children reach their potential. He was sceptical about issues of the day but kept faith in scripture and held up Jesus Christ as the model of the human person.

Albert Camus (1913-1960), a French Algerian from a poor family, developed existential humanism: the sense that life is absurd and has no meaning, because of routine, death, questioning and isolation. In The Outsider, Meursault's awareness of absurdity frees him and he finds happiness. In The Plague, citizens unite against a plague, showing human solidarity - 'there are more things to admire in man than to despise'. In The Fall, he is pessimistic, saying there is no forgiveness, only 'the judgement of men'. Camus believed meaning comes from respecting human dignity and fighting despair; he won the Nobel Prize in Literature.

rows.prompt: Examine the way in which one modern scientific theory about how the universe began could influence a person's understanding of the meaning of life.
rows.model_answer:
The Big Bang theory, developed by the Catholic priest George Lemaitre, says that the universe exploded into existence about 13.8 billion years ago. It is based on the second law of thermodynamics, which states that every day the universe becomes more disordered. Entropy, devised by Rudolf Clausius in 1850, measures this disorder. Brian Cox uses a sandcastle to show that ordered things almost always become disordered, which is why time runs one way - the Arrow of Time. Because a system eventually reaches thermodynamic equilibrium, the universe will die and cannot have existed forever, so there must have been a creation event. Newton's gravity and the centrifugal effect also suggest something set the universe in motion.

This could influence a person's understanding of meaning in different ways. It may challenge belief: how can a universe that will end in a Big Chill or Big Crunch be meaningful? Some may see no need for God as creator. However, others may see God as the first cause, what St Thomas Aquinas called the 'uncreated creator'. The fine tuning of the universe suggests care, not chance. Coyne says conflicts between science and religion are 'temporary and apparent'. The wonder of creation, as Pope Francis says in Laudato si', can lead people to see the world as 'a joyful mystery' and to care for the earth.

rows.prompt: Briefly outline the Expanding Universe theory of the cosmos.
rows.model_answer:
In the 1920s the American astronomer Edwin Hubble discovered that the galaxies were not falling together but were moving apart. This is the Expanding Universe theory. If the universe is expanding, it must have been smaller at some point in the past. The rate of expansion is decelerating (slowing down), which supports the view that there was an initial explosion that set the universe in motion.

Modern cosmology also holds that space itself was created in the Big Bang, and because space and time are closely linked, time began at that moment too - space and time exploded out of nothing. Scientists have discovered heat radiating from space, which is the leftover heat from the Big Bang. The theory is widely accepted by scientists and welcomed by most religious thinkers. However, there is no agreement about how the universe will end, and science has not yet discovered the cause of creation.
